pharm: Oral mutual prodrug (double ester) linking ampicillin and sulbactam; after absorption it is hydrolyzed in the gut wall to release the two agents in a 1:1 molar ratio. Ampicillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis while sulbactam irreversibly inhibits many beta-lactamases, restoring activity against beta-lactamase-producing organisms.
quick: May be taken with or without food
Use only if clearly needed; penicillins generally considered low risk
Small amounts in milk; monitor infant for diarrhea/rash
Reduce dosing frequency if CrCl <=30 mL/min
Caution; contraindicated if prior cholestatic jaundice with this drug
summary: Sultamicillin tosilate is an oral mutual prodrug of ampicillin plus the beta-lactamase inhibitor sulbactam, extending aminopenicillin coverage to many beta-lactamase-producing bacteria. Typical adult dosing is 375-750 mg twice daily for respiratory, ENT, urinary, skin/soft-tissue, and gynecologic infections, with a single 2.25 g dose option for uncomplicated gonorrhea. Key concerns are penicillin/beta-lactam hypersensitivity (including fatal anaphylaxis and cross-reactivity), Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and rash. Note: this agent is not FDA-approved; content here is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF sources.
indications: Upper respiratory tract infections including sinusitis, otitis media, and tonsillitis
Lower respiratory tract infections including bacterial pneumonia and bronchitis
Caused by susceptible beta-lactamase-producing organisms otherwise resistant to ampicillin alone

dosage.t: Every 12 hours, usually 5-14 days; continue 48 h after fever/symptoms resolve

dosage.d: 2.25 g as a single oral dose
dosage.n: Equivalent to six 375 mg or three 750 mg tablets
Children >=30 kg receive the usual adult dose

dosage.t: Lengthen the dosing interval per ampicillin practice
dosage.n: Ampicillin and sulbactam elimination are similarly prolonged

admin: Take orally; may be given with or without food
Swallow tablets whole; oral suspension available for those unable to take tablets
Confirm no penicillin or beta-lactam allergy before the first dose
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
In severe renal impairment, extend the dosing interval rather than the per-dose amount
moa: After oral absorption, sultamicillin is hydrolyzed by esterases in the intestinal wall to liberate ampicillin and sulbactam in equimolar amounts. Ampicillin binds penicillin-binding proteins to inhibit synthesis of the bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan, producing bactericidal activity. Sulbactam has little intrinsic antibacterial action but irreversibly inhibits many plasmid- and chromosomally-mediated beta-lactamases, protecting ampicillin from enzymatic degradation and restoring its activity against beta-lactamase-producing strains.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to penicillins, sulbactam, or any beta-lactam antibiotic
Previous history of cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with this drug (ampicillin/sulbactam)
relative: History of allergy to cephalosporins (possible cross-reactivity)
Infectious mononucleosis or lymphatic leukemia (high risk of skin rash - avoid)
History of any allergic diathesis or asthma
monitor: Signs of immediate hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis after dosing
Skin rash and, with prolonged therapy, hepatic, renal, and hematologic function

preg: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women; animal studies have not shown teratogenicity. Penicillins, including ampicillin/sulbactam, are generally regarded as having a low risk in pregnancy and may be used when clearly needed and the benefit justifies any potential risk.
lact: Ampicillin and sulbactam are excreted in human milk in low concentrations. Use with caution while breastfeeding; observe the infant for diarrhea, candidiasis, or rash/sensitization.
renal: In severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <=30 mL/min), elimination of both ampicillin and sulbactam is prolonged to a similar degree. Administer less frequently (lengthen the dosing interval) in line with usual practice for ampicillin.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; monitor liver function during prolonged therapy. Contraindicated in patients with a prior history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with ampicillin/sulbactam.

major: Allopurinol - substantially increased incidence of skin rash with concurrent aminopenicillin use
moderate: Probenecid - decreases renal tubular secretion, raising and prolonging ampicillin/sulbactam serum levels (sometimes used deliberately)
Bacteriostatic antibiotics (chloramphenicol, macrolides, tetracyclines, sulfonamides) - may antagonize the bactericidal effect of penicillins
Methotrexate - reduced renal clearance increasing methotrexate toxicity
Anticoagulants - penicillins may alter platelet aggregation and coagulation tests; monitor
minor: Oral contraceptives - reduced efficacy is possible; advise additional contraceptive precautions
Aminoglycosides - physically/chemically incompatible; do not mix, and effect may be reduced if combined inappropriately
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive urine glucose with non-enzymatic (copper-reduction) methods; high levels can interfere with some urinary protein assays.

serious: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis)
emergency: Severe/bloody diarrhea suggesting C. difficile colitis

monitoring: Hypersensitivity reactions, especially after the first dose
Diarrhea severity and duration; evaluate for C. difficile if severe or persistent
Hepatic, renal, and hematologic function during prolonged or high-dose therapy
Skin for rash, particularly in patients with mononucleosis or on allopurinol
Clinical response and signs of superinfection
counsel: Tell your clinician about any penicillin, cephalosporin, or other antibiotic allergy before starting
Stop the drug and seek emergency care for rash, swelling, wheezing, or trouble breathing
Report severe, watery, or bloody diarrhea, which can occur during or weeks after treatment
Finish the entire course even if you feel better, to avoid resistance and relapse
Use an additional non-hormonal contraceptive method if you take oral contraceptives
pk: Rapid absorption; therapeutic serum levels within ~1 hour
Peak plasma concentrations of ampicillin and sulbactam at ~0.9-1 hour
Ampicillin ~1 to 1.5 h; sulbactam ~1 to 1.3 h (both prolonged in renal impairment)
Supports twice-daily dosing; eliminated mainly by renal excretion
Store below 25-30 C in a dry place; protect from moisture (reconstituted suspension refrigerated, discard per label)
pearls: NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on EMA/SmPC (Pfizer UNASYN oral) and BNF/standard references for ampicillin/sulbactam
Oral bioavailability gives peak ampicillin levels roughly 2-3.5 times those of an equivalent dose of plain oral ampicillin
Ampicillin and sulbactam are released in a 1:1 molar ratio after intestinal hydrolysis of the prodrug
Avoid in suspected infectious mononucleosis - high incidence of maculopapular rash that is not true penicillin allergy
Allopurinol co-administration markedly increases the risk of rash
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the regular schedule; do not double up. Maintaining even spacing helps sustain antibacterial levels.
overdose: Limited data; high doses may cause gastrointestinal upset and, particularly in renal impairment, neurotoxicity with agitation, myoclonus, or seizures from beta-lactam accumulation. Management is supportive with symptomatic care and correction of fluid/electrolytes; both ampicillin and sulbactam are removed by hemodialysis, which can be used in severe overdose with renal failure.
